title: "4.1.6 Quinean Modal Skepticism"

Quine's modal skepticism is a thoroughgoing rejection of the modal vocabulary, and the position has not been refuted so much as outlasted by the literatures that find ways to work around it. "Two Dogmas of Empiricism" [-@quine1951] attacks the analytic/synthetic distinction on which much prior modal regimentation depended; "Reference and Modality" [-@quine1953] shows that quantifying into modal contexts produces the notorious failures of substitutivity that *de re* essentialism is supposed to license; *Word and Object* [-@quine1960] turns the screw further with the indeterminacy of translation, on which essential properties cannot be picked out across translation manuals. The proposed cure is austerity: keep the language of regimented science (extensional first-order logic, logic sensitive only to reference and truth-value, not to meaning or modal force, plus the working vocabulary of physics and biology), drop the language of necessity, get on with the work.

@follesdal1986 and @burgess1997 carry the position forward in modal logic; @gibbard1975 develops the contingent-identity wedge that presses against essentialism from within; Williamson's *Modal Logic as Metaphysics* [-@williamson2013, ch. 2] is the contemporary acknowledgment that the position remains the floor any modal account must clear. Where the present argument needs *de re* necessities (that the structural roles obtain in virtue of what they are, not in virtue of how we describe them) Quine's apparatus stands in the way.

The concession runs in full. Quine is right that mid-century modal regimentation imported analyticity as if Carnap had not been answered; right that quantification into modal contexts requires more than its proponents had supplied; right that translation does not pick out essences in any extensionally regimented way. The position closes more loose modal arguments than it opens, and any argument for necessary structural conditions has to clear the Quinean floor before it earns its conclusion. The Quinean tool has tracked something real about how modal vocabulary had been used; the question is whether it tracks something real about the structural conditions §2.6 establishes. Three forms of the Quinean move press the objection at three resolutions.

*First.* The classical analyticity form runs against the present account directly. Necessities, on this reading, are analytic in disguise: "Time is causally structured succession" is a stipulative truth about how we use "Time," not a discovery about what any change-permitting world contains. Modal claims trade on hidden synonymies, and once the synonymies are exposed there is nothing left for necessity to track. Gibbard's [-@gibbard1975] contingent-identity wedge sharpens the pressure: even paradigm *de re* identities can be analyzed as description-relative if essentialism is given up, and the *a posteriori* necessities the Kripkean apparatus delivers (water = H₂O) are recast as terminological decisions about which features fix reference.

The reply runs on the distinction between stipulative definition and structural specification. The role definitions of §§1.3–1.4 are not synonymy claims about how the English word "Time" relates to the English phrase "causally structured succession"; they are specifications of what any medium hosting transitions must instantiate, derived from what a transition consists in. The derivation does not depend on the term "Time" picking out anything in particular; it shows that succession, distinction, and exchange are the conditions on transition under any vocabulary in which the conditions can be stated. Quine's analyticity critique cuts against synonymy claims dressed up as discoveries; it leaves untouched discoveries that hold in any vocabulary capable of stating them. Gibbard's wedge cuts against essentialism construed as a discovery about which descriptions a thing satisfies; the present account is not in that business. It does not claim that *Time* picks out the same role across worlds; it shows that any world containing transitions instantiates the role, by whatever name.

*Second.* The *de re* / *de dicto* form presses where the first leaves off. Even granting that the structural conditions are not synonymy claims, the Quinean denies that the *de re* reading on which they obtain "of the world rather than of a description" is intelligible at all. Quantifying into modal contexts produces the failures @quine1953 catalogues: "necessarily, 9 is greater than 7" appears true, "9 = the number of planets" is true, "necessarily, the number of planets is greater than 7" is false. The *de re* reading on which a structural condition obtains *of* the medium, independent of how we describe it, is exactly the reading the substitutivity failures rule out. @follesdal1986 and @burgess1997 extend the point: modal logic is a useful instrument for organizing inferences but cannot, on Quinean grounds, be read off as picking out language-independent modal facts.

The reply concedes the substitutivity point and presses where it does not reach. The *de re* readings Quine's catalogue dismisses are readings on which a contingent description ("the number of planets") is treated as if it picked out its referent rigidly across modal contexts. The Kripkean apparatus (§4.1.1) answers the catalogue by distinguishing rigid from non-rigid designators; the present account does not depend on the answer. The structural roles are not picked out by a description that could have picked out something else; they are specified by what a transition requires, and the specification is invariant across the descriptions that satisfy it. There is no Quinean substitutivity failure to find because there is no substitution to perform: any term that satisfies the role-specification of Time picks out the same structural condition, and any term that fails to satisfy it picks out something else. The instrumentalist reading Burgess defends is consistent with this: modal logic is a useful instrument, and the structural conditions are what the instrument has to track to be useful. The instrument's utility on Burgess's own terms is the data the modal account explains.

*Third.* The extensional-regimentation form goes deepest. Even granting that the role-specifications hold in any vocabulary, the Quinean denies that the holding is *modal* in any sense that escapes extensional logic. What looks like necessity is the projectibility of certain predicates within our best science; what looks like *de re* essentialism is the privileged status of certain natural-kind classifications within that science. The work modal vocabulary did before is now done by what regimented science treats as nomological (law-governed, a matter of the laws of nature) and the question whether that treatment tracks something modally robust is exactly what Quine refuses to answer outside the framework. @williamson2013 [ch. 2] presses the contemporary form: the position survives as a methodological stance even where its first-order claims have been answered, and any necessitarian account has to show that the necessities it posits are not artifacts of the science that names them.

The reply distinguishes scope, and it discharges the burden several times over rather than resting on one bridge. The Quinean is right that much of what passed for modal claim at mid-century was projectibility-talk dressed up; right that natural-kind classifications carry methodological privilege within a science without thereby carrying language-independent modal weight; right that the burden is on the necessitarian. What the reply does *not* do is the thing the Quinean would be entitled to reject: assert that projectibility simply *is* structural necessity renamed. Quine has a fully naturalized account of projectibility (entrenched quality-spaces, "Natural Kinds," [-@quine1969b]); answering it by relabeling would beg the question. The conditions §2.6 identifies earn their standing instead by what any nomological practice must presuppose to be one at all, and several independent considerations converge on the same commitment.

*The transcendental consideration.* Actual projection occurs through succession and comparison among distinguishable cases, and Quine's naturalized story invokes persistence and causal selection. This establishes the structure of the actual scientific practice. It does not show that projectibility requires productive law-like causation rather than Humean regularity, or by itself establish the full loaded types in every possible world.

*The indispensability consideration.* Quine's own criterion fixes ontological commitment by what our best science must quantify over (§2.8.3). Any nomological practice quantifies ineliminably over a structured succession of distinguishable, causally interacting items; the structural conditions are not an optional modal overlay but what its bound variables range over. Quinean indispensability can commit the practice to whatever temporal, relational, and physical ontology its best regimentation genuinely quantifies over. Identifying that ontology exactly with the book's T, S, and Φ requires the independent role and realizer arguments; the criterion alone does not supply the identification.

*The invariance consideration.* What keeps the conditions from being artifacts of the science that names them (Williamson's [-@williamson2013, ch. 2] standing worry) is that *every* nomological practice presupposes them, not one. Rival sciences, future regimentations, and Quine's own meta-theory alike must range over them; none can decline them and remain nomological. Projectible predicates vary from science to science; the structural conditions do not, because they are the conditions under which any predicate is projectible at all. This is the thin framework-independence of §4.1.8: not a privileged carving beyond all frameworks, but conditions no framework can refuse.

The three considerations support a cumulative reply; none alone converts actual scientific practice into an unrestricted cross-world necessity. The work necessity did before is now done by what our best science treats as nomological, and what any nomological practice operates on, quantifies over, and cannot vary without ceasing to be nomological, is the structural conditions named.

A kindred move drops Quine's program for Williamson's necessitism [-@williamson2013], which keeps the modal vocabulary while denying that contingency is fundamental; that position is engaged at §4.4.6. A different skepticism keeps both the vocabulary and ordinary modal knowledge while denying that the modal faculty is reliable at metaphysical distances [@vanInwagen1998]; because it concedes everything the present section vindicates, it is engaged separately at §4.1.13. The adjacent deflationary tradition, modal conventionalism (§4.1.7) and metaontological deflationism (§4.1.8), runs parallel deflations at neighboring resolutions, and the structural reply takes the same form across the family. The regimentation of the structural claims in formal terms that satisfy Quine's extensionalist constraints is carried out at §§2.10.1–2.10.3, showing that the role-specifications are statable without the analytic/synthetic distinction and without quantifying into modal contexts in the way Quine's (1953) catalogue targets; the bound-variable ontology that licenses the existential commitments is laid out specifically at §2.8.3.

*What closes.* Three forms of Quinean austerity, and none opens the gap: the classical analyticity form cuts against synonymy dressed up as discovery and leaves structural specifications untouched; the *de re* / *de dicto* form catalogues substitutivity failures for contingent descriptions and leaves role-specifications, which admit no substitution, intact; and the extensional-regimentation form relocates necessity into nomological practice, reinstating the structural conditions as what any such practice operates on. The Quinean refuses the modal vocabulary; the present account shows what the vocabulary picks out, and what it picks out is unaltered by the refusal. However the austerity is run (as analyticity-skepticism, *de re* skepticism, or extensional regimentation) what each form contests is □(T∧S∧Φ) at the *a priori* / constitutive register, supported by the fixed-domain S5 lift from the Cartesian witness together with the separate Structural Requirement and role-to-type premises, the T5/N register line §4.1.1 records and §4.1.2 makes explicit.

The austerity has done genuine work, as the concession above records. What the austerity has not produced is a configuration of reality in which the structural conditions fail to obtain, and what the catalogue has not produced is a substitution failure that touches role-specification rather than description. The skepticism, taken seriously, narrows to the claim that necessity is an unnecessary word. The argument concedes the possibility and asks what remains when the word is gone. What remains is structure.
